case_name: CASE OF TSAAVA AND OTHERS v. GEORGIA

assessment.Applicability of Article 10: The clearest Article 10 issue arises in respect of the applicants who were reporting on the demonstration as journalists, camera operators and photographers (see paragraph 44). Their work consisted of observing, recording and transmitting information from an event of obvious public interest, namely a major anti-government protest outside Parliament. Newsgathering is an essential preparatory part of journalistic freedom, so injuries or coercive acts that stop journalists from filming or reporting amount to an interference with Article 10.

assessment.Context capable of justifying police int: The authorities did face a difficult and fast-moving situation. A substantial group of demonstrators repeatedly tried to break through the police cordon, seize equipment, throw objects and storm the Parliament building (see paragraphs 20-23, 29-31, 125-126). Preventing disorder and protecting Parliament and police officers were therefore legitimate aims. The broader background of the events has also been noted by the Court in related proceedings (see no. 13668/21). That context weighs in the State’s favour, but it does not remove the need for especially careful treatment of journalists and other non-violent persons.

assessment.Failure to distinguish journalists from: The facts strongly suggest that force was used against journalists who were not threatening anyone. Official video-analysis reports stated that Mr Tsaava, Mr Kmuzov and Mr Svanadze were calm and posed no danger when they were hit by kinetic impact projectiles (see paragraphs 47 and 51). Similar findings were made for Ms Baghashvili, Mr Muradov and Ms Abashidze, each of whom was recorded as posing no threat when injured (see paragraphs 54, 58 and 63). Several of them were visibly working with microphones, professional cameras, press cards or "Press" markings (see paragraphs 48, 54, 56-58, 60-62). This points to a failure to distinguish media workers from violent actors, despite domestic rules requiring that journalists not be impeded in their professional activity.

assessment.Serious impact on journalistic activity: The interference was not trivial. Ms Baghashvili suffered grave and life-threatening injuries, requiring surgery (see paragraph 70). Mr Muradov sustained multiple open wounds on his back and shoulder (see paragraph 75). Mr Koshkadze suffered facial wounds (see paragraph 76), and other journalist applicants suffered bruising, toxic effects of gas, or projectile injuries (see paragraphs 71-79). These injuries plainly disrupted or terminated their reporting at the scene. The domestic courts expressly found, in the cases of journalist applicants, that the injuries prevented them from continuing their professional duties during the demonstration (see paragraph 149).

assessment.Lack of adequate safeguards in the use o: The manner of dispersal appears incompatible with the strict scrutiny required where press freedom is affected. The first shooting and tear gas use at 11.55 p.m. were not preceded by a warning (see paragraph 32), while the first clear loudspeaker warning came only at 2.59 a.m., after hours of force had already been used (see paragraph 41). Kinetic impact projectiles were fired from above the stairs towards persons located further away (see paragraphs 34, 37 and 38). Domestic rules required prior warning, command authorisation for non-lethal projectiles, and prohibited simultaneous or parallel use of water cannon, tear gas and rubber bullets (see paragraphs 187-190). Yet the evidence suggests that officers used projectiles on their own initiative, without a specific order, and while tear gas was also being fired (see paragraphs 35, 123-126, 169 and 171). Such deficient planning and control are particularly problematic where journalists are present and identifiable.

assessment.Direct obstruction of a journalist insid: Mr Diasamidze’s case is especially significant for Article 10. He was a Parliament-accredited journalist (see paragraph 45) who had been helped by police into the inner courtyard and was livestreaming events from there (see paragraph 66). After identifying himself as a journalist and pointing to his badge, he was allegedly pushed, hit, threatened and expelled, while his equipment was interfered with and he was told to leave (see paragraphs 66-67 and 79). This was not crowd-control in the face of violent conduct by him; it was a direct obstruction of journalistic work by officers who knew, or should have known, his status.

assessment.Domestic findings reinforce the dispropo: Although the domestic civil judgments were not framed primarily under Article 10, they are highly relevant factually. The Tbilisi City Court, and in several cases the Court of Appeal, found that the police had used unnecessary and disproportionate force against peaceful claimants, including journalists, because they had not presented any danger (see paragraphs 149-156). Those findings substantially support the view that the interference with the journalists’ work was not 'necessary in a democratic society'.

assessment.Overall assessment under Article 10: Even allowing for the violent conduct of part of the crowd, the material indicates that journalists covering a matter of exceptional public interest were struck by projectiles, exposed to gas, or physically removed despite being calm, visible and engaged in reporting (see paragraphs 47, 51, 54, 58, 63 and 66). The authorities did not show that such interference was narrowly targeted, preceded by adequate safeguards, or limited to what was strictly necessary. On the contrary, the evidence points to indiscriminate or poorly controlled force that foreseeably prevented media coverage. That is likely to be regarded by the Court as a breach of Article 10.
